domain.title: AI Lifecycle & Systems Governance
domain.outcome: Integrate D04 knowledge into defensible AI-governance analysis, professional artifacts and accountable decisions.

modules.title: AI Lifecycle Foundations
modules.whyThisMatters: Deployment is not the only point at which risk is created. Early problem framing and later change or decommissioning decisions can affect people as much as model performance.
learningObjectives: Explain lifecycle stages and interacting model, system, product, software, data and governance lifecycles; identify gates, owners, evidence and escalation; create five lifecycle governance artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: AI systems are governed across a lifecycle that begins with a problem and continues through data, development, validation, deployment, operation, monitoring, change and retirement.

content.explanation: AI lifecycle is a governance question that must be answered with context, evidence, decision rights, stakeholder analysis and lifecycle timing. Organizations may use different labels, but the professional obligation is to make the decision and its basis traceable.
content.worked_example: A European insurer maps problem definition, data preparation, model development, deployment, monitoring and retirement, with a gate before each material decision.
content.governance_implication: A gate owner records what is approved, what remains uncertain, what evidence is required, and what would trigger escalation or review.
content.professional_application: Use AI lifecycle in a lifecycle map, proposal, register, gate, assessment, approval record or development control.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map the full lifecycle and identify gates before work starts. At each gate define purpose, owner, evidence, risks, affected stakeholders, approval criteria and next action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public-sector, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; do not assume one lifecycle vocabulary or operating model.

Compare regions and organizational maturity without treating one jurisdiction as the universal model. Resource constraints may change sequencing and evidence methods, but not the need for accountable decisions.

cases.title: The gate that was skipped
cases.context: The organization operates across sectors and regions with different levels of technical maturity, data availability and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A lifecycle-managed AI service involving data acquisition, model development, human decisions, deployment and monitoring.
cases.governance_problem: A model moves from prototype to production without a documented purpose, approval owner or retirement condition.
evidence: the problem and intended purpose are documented
data and system boundaries are partly defined
stakeholder needs and harms are unevenly understood
resources and specialist capacity are limited
cases.decision_point: Whether to pause deployment and reconstruct lifecycle decisions.
cases.analysis: Clarify whether AI is suitable, identify decision rights and lifecycle gates, assess data and stakeholder effects, define controls and evidence, and record uncertainty and alternatives.
cases.governance_response: Use a proportionate gate; approve, condition, redesign, defer or reject based on evidence. Assign owners, document limitations, require human oversight and establish monitoring and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is a sequence of accountable decisions, not a technical checklist performed only before launch.

modules.title: Problem Definition & Use-Case Governance
modules.whyThisMatters: A poorly framed use case can make every later technical decision irrelevant. An organization may need a non-AI alternative, a narrower purpose, stronger human review or a no-go decision.
learningObjectives: Define and justify a problem; distinguish problem from solution; assess AI suitability, alternatives, benefits, harms and stakeholders; classify use cases; conduct go/no-go, conditional approval, redesign, deferral and rejection decisions; create seven artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Good AI governance begins by deciding whether the problem is real, whether AI is suitable and whether the proposed use is necessary, proportionate and governable.

content.explanation: problem definition is a governance question that must be answered with context, evidence, decision rights, stakeholder analysis and lifecycle timing. Organizations may use different labels, but the professional obligation is to make the decision and its basis traceable.
content.worked_example: A European insurer maps problem definition, data preparation, model development, deployment, monitoring and retirement, with a gate before each material decision.
content.governance_implication: A gate owner records what is approved, what remains uncertain, what evidence is required, and what would trigger escalation or review.
content.professional_application: Use problem definition in a lifecycle map, proposal, register, gate, assessment, approval record or development control.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map the full lifecycle and identify gates before work starts. At each gate define purpose, owner, evidence, risks, affected stakeholders, approval criteria and next action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public-sector, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; do not assume one lifecycle vocabulary or operating model.

Compare regions and organizational maturity without treating one jurisdiction as the universal model. Resource constraints may change sequencing and evidence methods, but not the need for accountable decisions.

cases.title: The solution looking for a problem
cases.context: The organization operates across sectors and regions with different levels of technical maturity, data availability and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A lifecycle-managed AI service involving data acquisition, model development, human decisions, deployment and monitoring.
cases.governance_problem: A department proposes an AI risk score for social-service triage, but the actual problem may be solved by staffing and process redesign.
evidence: the problem and intended purpose are documented
data and system boundaries are partly defined
stakeholder needs and harms are unevenly understood
resources and specialist capacity are limited
cases.decision_point: Whether to approve, narrow, redesign or reject the AI use case.
cases.analysis: Clarify whether AI is suitable, identify decision rights and lifecycle gates, assess data and stakeholder effects, define controls and evidence, and record uncertainty and alternatives.
cases.governance_response: Use a proportionate gate; approve, condition, redesign, defer or reject based on evidence. Assign owners, document limitations, require human oversight and establish monitoring and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is a sequence of accountable decisions, not a technical checklist performed only before launch.

knowledgeChecks.question: A process problem may be solved without AI. What should happen?
options: Document the purpose, evidence, owner and decision gate
Start development because AI is fashionable
Assume data quality is universal
Leave the decision undocumented
knowledgeChecks.correct_answer: Document the purpose, evidence, owner and decision gate
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Lifecycle governance makes decisions traceable from problem definition through data, development, deployment, operation, change and retirement.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: A defensible answer addresses accountability, proportionality, stakeholder impact and evidence rather than treating technology as the starting point.

modules.title: Data Governance
modules.whyThisMatters: Poor data governance creates privacy, security, bias, IP, safety and operational risks that model tuning cannot repair.
learningObjectives: Define ownership, stewardship, provenance, lineage and accountability; govern acquisition, preparation, transformation, storage, access, sharing, retention and deletion; assess contextual data quality; govern training, validation, test, production, labels, metadata, synthetic, retrieved, user and feedback data; create eight artifacts.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map the full lifecycle and identify gates before work starts. At each gate define purpose, owner, evidence, risks, affected stakeholders, approval criteria and next action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public-sector, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; do not assume one lifecycle vocabulary or operating model.

Compare regions and organizational maturity without treating one jurisdiction as the universal model. Resource constraints may change sequencing and evidence methods, but not the need for accountable decisions.

cases.title: The complete dataset that was incomplete
cases.context: The organization operates across sectors and regions with different levels of technical maturity, data availability and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A lifecycle-managed AI service involving data acquisition, model development, human decisions, deployment and monitoring.
cases.governance_problem: A dataset is technically large but excludes rural patients and contains unclear provenance and outdated labels.
evidence: the problem and intended purpose are documented
data and system boundaries are partly defined
stakeholder needs and harms are unevenly understood
resources and specialist capacity are limited
cases.decision_point: Whether it is fit for purpose and what controls are needed.
cases.analysis: Clarify whether AI is suitable, identify decision rights and lifecycle gates, assess data and stakeholder effects, define controls and evidence, and record uncertainty and alternatives.
cases.governance_response: Use a proportionate gate; approve, condition, redesign, defer or reject based on evidence. Assign owners, document limitations, require human oversight and establish monitoring and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is a sequence of accountable decisions, not a technical checklist performed only before launch.

modules.title: Dataset Quality & Provenance
modules.whyThisMatters: A dataset may be large, recent or licensed and still be unsuitable because of sampling, labels, leakage, contamination, missing groups or undocumented transformations.
learningObjectives: Evaluate fitness for purpose; trace sources, collection, transformation, annotation, version and access; document composition, limitations and prohibited uses; identify bias, missingness, imbalance, duplicates, stale data, contamination and leakage; govern synthetic and augmented data; create seven artifacts.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map the full lifecycle and identify gates before work starts. At each gate define purpose, owner, evidence, risks, affected stakeholders, approval criteria and next action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public-sector, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; do not assume one lifecycle vocabulary or operating model.

Compare regions and organizational maturity without treating one jurisdiction as the universal model. Resource constraints may change sequencing and evidence methods, but not the need for accountable decisions.

evidence: the problem and intended purpose are documented

cases.decision_point: Whether it is fit for a new hiring purpose and how provenance should be documented.
cases.analysis: Clarify whether AI is suitable, identify decision rights and lifecycle gates, assess data and stakeholder effects, define controls and evidence, and record uncertainty and alternatives.
cases.governance_response: Use a proportionate gate; approve, condition, redesign, defer or reject based on evidence. Assign owners, document limitations, require human oversight and establish monitoring and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is a sequence of accountable decisions, not a technical checklist performed only before launch.

modules.title: Model Development Governance
modules.whyThisMatters: Uncontrolled experimentation and undocumented changes make models irreproducible, unsafe and difficult to review. Governance should support innovation while preserving requirements, peer review, evidence and decision gates.
learningObjectives: Define model objectives and requirements; govern architecture, selection, training, fine-tuning, feature engineering, parameters, experimentation, environments, version control and reproducibility; address development risks and controls across traditional ML, deep learning, generative, foundation, retrieval and agentic systems; create eight artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Model development governance makes experimentation, training, architecture, versioning, testing and approval accountable before a model becomes a deployed system.

content.explanation: model development lifecycle is a governance question that must be answered with context, evidence, decision rights, stakeholder analysis and lifecycle timing. Organizations may use different labels, but the professional obligation is to make the decision and its basis traceable.
content.worked_example: A European insurer maps problem definition, data preparation, model development, deployment, monitoring and retirement, with a gate before each material decision.
content.governance_implication: A gate owner records what is approved, what remains uncertain, what evidence is required, and what would trigger escalation or review.
content.professional_application: Use model development lifecycle in a lifecycle map, proposal, register, gate, assessment, approval record or development control.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map the full lifecycle and identify gates before work starts. At each gate define purpose, owner, evidence, risks, affected stakeholders, approval criteria and next action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public-sector, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; do not assume one lifecycle vocabulary or operating model.

Compare regions and organizational maturity without treating one jurisdiction as the universal model. Resource constraints may change sequencing and evidence methods, but not the need for accountable decisions.

cases.title: The experiment no one could reproduce
cases.context: The organization operates across sectors and regions with different levels of technical maturity, data availability and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A lifecycle-managed AI service involving data acquisition, model development, human decisions, deployment and monitoring.
cases.governance_problem: A promising model cannot be recreated because code, data, configuration and environment versions were not recorded.
evidence: the problem and intended purpose are documented
data and system boundaries are partly defined
stakeholder needs and harms are unevenly understood
resources and specialist capacity are limited
cases.decision_point: Whether to approve further testing or require reconstruction.
cases.analysis: Clarify whether AI is suitable, identify decision rights and lifecycle gates, assess data and stakeholder effects, define controls and evidence, and record uncertainty and alternatives.
cases.governance_response: Use a proportionate gate; approve, condition, redesign, defer or reject based on evidence. Assign owners, document limitations, require human oversight and establish monitoring and review.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is a sequence of accountable decisions, not a technical checklist performed only before launch.

modules.title: Testing & Validation
modules.whyThisMatters: Unexamined assumptions, narrow datasets and unclear acceptance criteria can let unsafe or unsuitable systems pass into operation.
learningObjectives: Distinguish testing, validation, verification and evaluation; design pre/post-deployment tests; cover data, model and system criteria; plan functional, performance, safety, security, fairness, privacy, factuality, oversight, adversarial, negative, boundary, stress and regression tests; govern generative and agentic testing; create nine artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Testing and validation are formal governance activities that establish whether an AI system meets defined requirements and criteria under defined conditions.

content.explanation: testing is a governance practice that requires defined purpose, scope, criteria, evidence, decision rights and follow-up. A metric, approval or version label has meaning only in its operating context.
content.worked_example: A European public-service team rejects a single accuracy threshold and adds subgroup, safety, override and incident criteria before deployment.
content.governance_implication: The practitioner records what was examined, what remains uncertain, who decides, what action follows and what would trigger review.
content.professional_application: Apply testing in a strategy, gate checklist, oversight workflow, monitoring register, change request or post-change review.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define scope and criteria before selecting metrics, gates or approvals. Include affected people, system boundaries, evidence quality, uncertainty, reversibility and escalation.
Use proportionate controls across enterprise, government, regulated, technology, civil-society and research contexts; compare regions without assuming one default model.
Where testing or monitoring resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable populations, safety/security concerns, high-impact changes and signals that can trigger action.

cases.title: The passing benchmark
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different infrastructure, technical maturity, user expectations and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A production AI service with human users, monitoring, data and model dependencies, operational controls and change events.
cases.governance_problem: Aggregate performance passes but factuality, subgroup error and prompt-injection tests are incomplete.
evidence: pre-deployment evidence exists but coverage is uneven
production telemetry is incomplete or delayed
human workload and user understanding vary
model, data, vendor or policy changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether to approve, restrict or extend validation before release.
cases.analysis: Define criteria, inspect evidence, examine uncertainty and affected groups, assess readiness or performance, assign decision rights, and determine whether to approve, constrain, roll back, escalate or reassess.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate or trigger with explicit owner, evidence, threshold, escalation, remediation, rollback and review requirements.
cases.lessons_learned: Testing, deployment, oversight, monitoring and change governance are connected decisions rather than separate technical activities.

modules.title: Deployment Governance
modules.whyThisMatters: A technically functional model can fail because infrastructure, support, training, monitoring, privacy, security or rollback are not ready.
learningObjectives: Assess readiness and approve deployment; design gates for internal, cloud, API, embedded, third-party, edge, on-premise, hybrid, public and employee-facing AI; govern pilots, phased rollout, rollback, pause and emergency shutdown; create seven artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Deployment governance is the evidence-based transition from development to operational use. It combines technical, risk, compliance, operational, organizational, user and assurance readiness.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define scope and criteria before selecting metrics, gates or approvals. Include affected people, system boundaries, evidence quality, uncertainty, reversibility and escalation.
Use proportionate controls across enterprise, government, regulated, technology, civil-society and research contexts; compare regions without assuming one default model.
Where testing or monitoring resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable populations, safety/security concerns, high-impact changes and signals that can trigger action.

cases.title: Ready in the lab, unready in production
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different infrastructure, technical maturity, user expectations and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A production AI service with human users, monitoring, data and model dependencies, operational controls and change events.
cases.governance_problem: The model passes validation but support, monitoring, user training and incident escalation are not operational.
evidence: pre-deployment evidence exists but coverage is uneven
production telemetry is incomplete or delayed
human workload and user understanding vary
model, data, vendor or policy changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether to pilot, delay, conditionally approve or reject deployment.
cases.analysis: Define criteria, inspect evidence, examine uncertainty and affected groups, assess readiness or performance, assign decision rights, and determine whether to approve, constrain, roll back, escalate or reassess.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate or trigger with explicit owner, evidence, threshold, escalation, remediation, rollback and review requirements.
cases.lessons_learned: Testing, deployment, oversight, monitoring and change governance are connected decisions rather than separate technical activities.

modules.title: Human Oversight
modules.whyThisMatters: A nominal human in the workflow may rubber-stamp outputs or lack the ability to correct them. Oversight must be designed and tested as an operational control.
learningObjectives: Distinguish human-in-the-loop, on-the-loop, in-command and meaningful human control; design decision rights, intervention, override, escalation, supervision, explanations, workload, uncertainty communication and effectiveness assessment; address automation bias in high-impact sectors without unsupported legal claims.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define scope and criteria before selecting metrics, gates or approvals. Include affected people, system boundaries, evidence quality, uncertainty, reversibility and escalation.
Use proportionate controls across enterprise, government, regulated, technology, civil-society and research contexts; compare regions without assuming one default model.
Where testing or monitoring resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable populations, safety/security concerns, high-impact changes and signals that can trigger action.

cases.title: The reviewer who could not review
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different infrastructure, technical maturity, user expectations and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A production AI service with human users, monitoring, data and model dependencies, operational controls and change events.
cases.governance_problem: Caseworkers receive opaque recommendations, have little time and are evaluated on throughput, so overrides are rare.
evidence: pre-deployment evidence exists but coverage is uneven
production telemetry is incomplete or delayed
human workload and user understanding vary
model, data, vendor or policy changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether oversight is meaningful and how to redesign the workflow.
cases.analysis: Define criteria, inspect evidence, examine uncertainty and affected groups, assess readiness or performance, assign decision rights, and determine whether to approve, constrain, roll back, escalate or reassess.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate or trigger with explicit owner, evidence, threshold, escalation, remediation, rollback and review requirements.
cases.lessons_learned: Testing, deployment, oversight, monitoring and change governance are connected decisions rather than separate technical activities.

modules.title: Monitoring & Performance Management
modules.whyThisMatters: Accuracy, latency or availability alone may miss drift, subgroup harm, privacy, safety, factuality, complaints, overrides or operational failure.
learningObjectives: Design post-deployment, performance, operational, risk, data, model, user, system and governance monitoring; select contextual metrics; detect data, concept and model drift; set warning, alert and escalation thresholds; analyze trends, subgroups, incidents and remediation; create seven artifacts.

contentSections.content: Post-deployment monitoring turns an AI system from a one-time approval into an observable, reviewable service. Metrics must match purpose and lead to action.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define scope and criteria before selecting metrics, gates or approvals. Include affected people, system boundaries, evidence quality, uncertainty, reversibility and escalation.
Use proportionate controls across enterprise, government, regulated, technology, civil-society and research contexts; compare regions without assuming one default model.
Where testing or monitoring resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable populations, safety/security concerns, high-impact changes and signals that can trigger action.

content: A European public-service team rejects a single accuracy threshold and adds subgroup, safety, override and incident criteria before deployment.
A Southeast Asian retailer begins with a controlled pilot, trains users, monitors complaints and retains rollback evidence before expanding.

cases.title: The metric that looked healthy
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different infrastructure, technical maturity, user expectations and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A production AI service with human users, monitoring, data and model dependencies, operational controls and change events.
cases.governance_problem: Accuracy and uptime remain stable while complaints and adverse outcomes rise for a subgroup after population behavior changes.
evidence: pre-deployment evidence exists but coverage is uneven
production telemetry is incomplete or delayed
human workload and user understanding vary
model, data, vendor or policy changes may occur
cases.decision_point: Whether to investigate, adjust thresholds, restrict use or remediate.
cases.analysis: Define criteria, inspect evidence, examine uncertainty and affected groups, assess readiness or performance, assign decision rights, and determine whether to approve, constrain, roll back, escalate or reassess.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate or trigger with explicit owner, evidence, threshold, escalation, remediation, rollback and review requirements.
cases.lessons_learned: Testing, deployment, oversight, monitoring and change governance are connected decisions rather than separate technical activities.

modules.title: Change & Version Governance
modules.whyThisMatters: A small change can create a large effect in a consequential system, while not every software change needs the same approval. Governance must classify change, assess impact, test, approve, deploy, roll back, document and monitor.
learningObjectives: Design change and configuration governance; version models, datasets, code, prompts, retrieval sources, APIs, infrastructure, policies and systems; classify minor, material, major and emergency changes; assess risk, performance, safety, security, privacy, fairness, legal, user, operational and assurance impacts; create seven artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview
contentSections.content: Change and version governance makes updates to models, data, code, prompts, APIs, infrastructure, policies and interfaces reviewable and proportionate to their impact.

content.explanation: change governance is a governance practice that requires defined purpose, scope, criteria, evidence, decision rights and follow-up. A metric, approval or version label has meaning only in its operating context.
content.worked_example: A European public-service team rejects a single accuracy threshold and adds subgroup, safety, override and incident criteria before deployment.
content.governance_implication: The practitioner records what was examined, what remains uncertain, who decides, what action follows and what would trigger review.
content.professional_application: Apply change governance in a strategy, gate checklist, oversight workflow, monitoring register, change request or post-change review.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Define scope and criteria before selecting metrics, gates or approvals. Include affected people, system boundaries, evidence quality, uncertainty, reversibility and escalation.
Use proportionate controls across enterprise, government, regulated, technology, civil-society and research contexts; compare regions without assuming one default model.
Where testing or monitoring resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, vulnerable populations, safety/security concerns, high-impact changes and signals that can trigger action.

content: A European public-service team rejects a single accuracy threshold and adds subgroup, safety, override and incident criteria before deployment.
A Southeast Asian retailer begins with a controlled pilot, trains users, monitors complaints and retains rollback evidence before expanding.
A West African health service classifies a vendor model update as material because local-language performance and human workload may change.

cases.title: The prompt change that changed decisions
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different infrastructure, technical maturity, user expectations and governance capacity.
cases.ai_system: A production AI service with human users, monitoring, data and model dependencies, operational controls and change events.
cases.governance_problem: A prompt update alters refusal and recommendation behavior but is treated as a minor copy change.
evidence: pre-deployment evidence exists but coverage is uneven
production telemetry is incomplete or delayed
human workload and user understanding vary
model, data, vendor or policy changes may occur
cases.decision_point: How to classify, test, approve and monitor the change.
cases.analysis: Define criteria, inspect evidence, examine uncertainty and affected groups, assess readiness or performance, assign decision rights, and determine whether to approve, constrain, roll back, escalate or reassess.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate or trigger with explicit owner, evidence, threshold, escalation, remediation, rollback and review requirements.
cases.lessons_learned: Testing, deployment, oversight, monitoring and change governance are connected decisions rather than separate technical activities.

modules.title: Decommissioning & Retirement
modules.whyThisMatters: A system can create harm after it is “turned off” if credentials remain active, records disappear, users lose services, replacement validation is weak or dependencies are overlooked.
learningObjectives: Distinguish deactivation, suspension, retirement, decommissioning, replacement, withdrawal and shutdown; identify triggers; govern authority, notification, data, records, access, infrastructure, vendors, migration, parallel operation, validation, rollback and post-retirement review; create nine artifacts.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map lifecycle stages, actors, dependencies, gates, evidence and decision rights before selecting controls or approving action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; compare global contexts without imposing one jurisdiction as universal.
Where resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, affected stakeholders, evidence preservation, operational continuity, security, privacy and reversible transitions.

modules.whyThisMatters: When requirements, data, versions, tests, approvals, incidents and changes cannot be linked, accountability becomes retrospective guesswork.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map lifecycle stages, actors, dependencies, gates, evidence and decision rights before selecting controls or approving action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; compare global contexts without imposing one jurisdiction as universal.
Where resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, affected stakeholders, evidence preservation, operational continuity, security, privacy and reversible transitions.

cases.title: The decision with no evidence chain
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different technical maturity, infrastructure, vendor dependence and stakeholder expectations.
cases.ai_system: A lifecycle-managed AI service with data, model, human, vendor, integration, monitoring, change and retirement dependencies.
cases.governance_problem: A regulator asks why a model was approved, but the organization cannot link the decision to data, tests, controls or the deployed version.
evidence: lifecycle records exist but are incomplete
system and vendor dependencies are material
stakeholder impacts vary by region and use
resources for documentation, monitoring or transition are limited
cases.decision_point: How to reconstruct and remediate traceability.
cases.analysis: Trace the issue to lifecycle stage, actor, risk, control, evidence, decision authority and downstream impact. Compare alternatives and record uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate, approval, escalation, transition, monitoring or retirement action with named owner, evidence requirements, stakeholder communication and review conditions.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is an accountable chain from problem definition to retirement, not a collection of disconnected documents.

modules.title: Vendor & System Integration Governance
modules.whyThisMatters: Interface and dependency failures can propagate beyond the model. Contracts, architecture maps and end-to-end testing must make fallback, failure and change manageable.
learningObjectives: Map system, trust, data and dependency boundaries; assess interface, data-flow, security, privacy, performance, availability, lock-in, concentration, version, propagation and vendor risks; govern due diligence, contracts, testing, fallback, graceful degradation and resilience; create eight artifacts.

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map lifecycle stages, actors, dependencies, gates, evidence and decision rights before selecting controls or approving action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; compare global contexts without imposing one jurisdiction as universal.
Where resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, affected stakeholders, evidence preservation, operational continuity, security, privacy and reversible transitions.

modules.title: End-to-End Lifecycle Control
modules.whyThisMatters: Siloed controls create gaps at handoffs. A lifecycle architecture makes decision rights, evidence, escalation and monitoring coherent across the whole system.
learningObjectives: Design lifecycle governance, control, gate, accountability, evidence, escalation and monitoring architectures; define eight gates with entry criteria, evidence, authority, risks, conditions, escalation and exit criteria; map Risk → Control Objective → Control → Owner → Evidence → Monitoring → Review; create eight artifacts.

contentSections.label: Overview

contentSections.label: Governance practice
content: Map lifecycle stages, actors, dependencies, gates, evidence and decision rights before selecting controls or approving action.
Use proportionate governance across enterprise, public, regulated, technology, civil-society and research settings; compare global contexts without imposing one jurisdiction as universal.
Where resources are limited, prioritize consequential decisions, affected stakeholders, evidence preservation, operational continuity, security, privacy and reversible transitions.

cases.title: The gap between gates
cases.context: The organization operates across regions and sectors with different technical maturity, infrastructure, vendor dependence and stakeholder expectations.
cases.ai_system: A lifecycle-managed AI service with data, model, human, vendor, integration, monitoring, change and retirement dependencies.
cases.governance_problem: Each team meets its local checklist, but no one owns the handoff from testing to deployment or from change to retirement.
evidence: lifecycle records exist but are incomplete
system and vendor dependencies are material
stakeholder impacts vary by region and use
resources for documentation, monitoring or transition are limited
cases.decision_point: How to design an integrated control architecture and accountability model.
cases.analysis: Trace the issue to lifecycle stage, actor, risk, control, evidence, decision authority and downstream impact. Compare alternatives and record uncertainty.
cases.governance_response: Use a gate, approval, escalation, transition, monitoring or retirement action with named owner, evidence requirements, stakeholder communication and review conditions.
cases.lessons_learned: Lifecycle governance is an accountable chain from problem definition to retirement, not a collection of disconnected documents.
